advances: The proposed planar integer-superlevel count comparison fails even for a rational triangle and a strictly positive affine radius whose global maximum is attained at a unique integer point. Thus concavity and an actual integer peak alone do not give the proposed constant-mass high-radius core count estimate. This is an obstruction to that bounded counting route, not a disproof of the locked Weak Oertel target.
author: research-agent
proof:
The triangle has the exact closed description
\(P_M=\{(x,y):0\le y\le1,\ 0\le x\le My\}\).
Indeed, for any point satisfying these inequalities, the coefficients
\(1-y\), \(y-x/M\), and \(x/M\) are nonnegative, sum to one, and express it as a convex combination of \((0,0),(0,1),(M,1)\). Conversely, each such convex combination satisfies the inequalities. The vertices are rational and noncollinear for \(M\ge1\), so \(P_M\) is rational, compact, convex, and full dimensional.

The function \(r_M=2-y\) is affine and takes values in \([1,2]\) throughout this triangle. Since its value decreases with \(y\), its global maximum can occur only when \(y=0\). The displayed description then forces \(x=0\). Thus the maximum is uniquely attained at \(z_0=(0,0)\), with value \(R_M=2\); in particular this is an actual integer peak, not a peak between integer points.

If \((x,y)\in P_M\cap\mathbb Z^2\), the bounds \(0\le y\le1\) force \(y\in\{0,1\}\). At \(y=0\), the only possible point is \((0,0)\). At \(y=1\), the possibilities are exactly \((k,1)\) for \(k=0,1,\ldots,M\). Hence the entire original integer support, including every boundary point, is
\(P_M\cap\mathbb Z^2=\{(0,0)\}\cup\{(k,1):0\le k\le M,\ k\in\mathbb Z\}\).
The radius is \(2\) at the first point and \(1\) at each of the remaining \(M+1\) points. This proves the stated formula for \(N_M(t)\), with all top-edge points included when \(t=1/2\) because the superlevel inequality is non-strict.

At \(t=1/2\), all \(M+2\) integer points are counted. At \(1-\delta=3/4\), the threshold is \((3/4)R_M=3/2\), so only \((0,0)\) is counted. Also \(1+(1-t)/\delta=1+(1/2)/(1/4)=3\). The proposed inequality would therefore require \(M+2\le9C\). For any finite \(C\ge0\), choose an integer \(M\ge1\) with \(M+2>9C\); this contradicts the inequality. A negative \(C\) cannot satisfy it either, because the counts are positive. All comparisons above are exact counts in the original integer lattice; no volume comparison or smoothing estimate is used.
statement:
For each integer \(M\ge1\), define the rational compact convex triangle
\(P_M=\operatorname{conv}\{(0,0),(0,1),(M,1)\}\subset\mathbb R^2\)
and the affine, hence concave, function \(r_M(x,y)=2-y\) on \(P_M\).
It is strictly positive on all of \(P_M\), and its values at integer points are positive integers. Its maximum over \(P_M\), and therefore its integer maximum, is \(R_M=2\), attained uniquely at the actual integer point \(z_0=(0,0)\).

With boundaries included, let
\(N_M(t)=\#\{z\in P_M\cap\mathbb Z^2:r_M(z)\ge tR_M\}\) for \(0\le t\le1\). Then
\[
N_M(t)=
\begin{cases}
M+2,&0\le t\le\tfrac12,\\
1,&\tfrac12<t\le1.
\end{cases}
\]
Consequently, at the fixed choices \(t=1/2\) and \(\delta=1/4\),
\[
\frac{N_M(t)}{\bigl(1+(1-t)/\delta\bigr)^2N_M(1-\delta)}
=\frac{M+2}{9}\longrightarrow\infty.
\]
There is therefore no finite dimension-only constant \(C\) for which the proposed comparison holds for all such planar \(P,r\), all \(0<\delta<1\), and all \(t\in[0,1]\).
